comparison: Both strongly support PGAM1 upregulation in Tregs. OpenEval (C1-C3, C13-C15) and peer review (C1-C3, C10-C11, C13-C15, C44) both accept the RNA-seq, scRNA-seq, and proteomics evidence. Peer review additionally includes the suppressive Treg subset analysis (C10-C11, C44) in this grouping, while OpenEval addresses these separately in R2.

OpenEval R2 addresses PGAM1 in suppressive TIL-Treg subsets (C10-C11, C44, C73) as a separate supported finding. Peer review R1 includes these claims (C10-C11, C44) together with the general PGAM1 upregulation data, treating them as part of the same evidence base for PGAM enrichment.

Both support the pharmacological and genetic inhibition findings (C4-C6, C45). OpenEval includes additional methodological details (C54, C71-C72) about viability and proliferation controls. Peer reviewers explicitly note the 'rigorous' use of inhibitors and antisense RNA without raising concerns.

Both support transcriptional changes from PGAM inhibition (C7-C8). OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of RNA-seq, PCA, and GSEA data. Peer review R3 implicitly accepts these findings as part of identifying 'new metabolic regulation' without specific critique.

OpenEval R5 addresses functional suppression assay data (C9) as separate supported evidence. Peer review R3 implicitly includes functional data in their acceptance of PGAM's role in Treg function, though not explicitly discussed.

Both support the opposing GAPDH effect (C12). OpenEval notes the finding demonstrates nuanced glycolytic regulation with somewhat speculative mechanistic interpretation (C49-C50, C70). Peer review accepts this as part of overall evidence without specific discussion.

Both support the serine metabolomics findings (C16-C18). OpenEval emphasizes mass spectrometry and isotope tracing data with mechanistic context (C43, C59-C60). Peer review R5 includes these claims with the rescue experiments, accepting the serine synthesis link.

Both strongly support the mechanistic rescue experiments (C19-C21, C46). OpenEval highlights convergent evidence from PHGDH inhibition, 3PG supplementation, and PHGDH knockdown. Peer reviewer 1 explicitly confirms understanding and acceptance of the PHGDH rescue experiments.

Perfect agreement on serine supplementation effects (C22-C23). Both support the finding that exogenous serine decreases Treg differentiation. Peer reviewer 1 explicitly notes the authors tested both synthesized and exogenous serine effects.

Perfect agreement on dietary serine restriction in vivo (C24-C25, C48). Both support increased peripheral Tregs and reduced EAE severity. Reviewers 1 and 2 explicitly note the in vivo experiments, and editor confirms solid evidence from mouse models.

OpenEval rates SCFEA computational predictions (C26-C29, C75) as UNCERTAIN due to reliance on computational modeling without direct flux measurements. Peer review R8 implicitly accepts these analyses as part of overall evidence base without specific discussion or concerns about the computational nature.

Both support one-carbon metabolism mechanism (C30-C32). OpenEval includes biochemical context (C62-C63). Peer reviewer 1 explicitly confirms understanding that serine effects depend on one-carbon metabolism and DNA methylation contributions.

OpenEval R13 addresses isotope tracing into methylcytosine and TSDR methylation (C33-C36, C76) as strongly supported. Peer review R9 includes C33 with the broader one-carbon metabolism findings (C30-C32, C47), accepting the methylation mechanism.

OpenEval R13 includes TSDR methylation data (C34-C36). Peer review R10 addresses site-specific CpG methylation changes (C34-C35, C36-C38), accepting the serine-methylation link as part of the proposed mechanism.

Both support site-specific methylation findings (C37-C38). OpenEval notes functional consequences of individual CpG changes not directly tested. Peer review accepts these findings as supporting the overall mechanism that serine induces methylation of Treg-associated genes.

Both strongly support methylation inhibition enhancing Treg function (C39-C42). OpenEval includes additional claims (C47, C77) about mechanisms. Peer reviewer 2 and editor confirm in vivo colitis model validation, accepting the complete mechanistic pathway.

OpenEval R6 addresses GAPDH vs PGAM opposing effects with mechanistic interpretation (C12, C49-C50, C70). Peer review R12 focuses on the overall conceptual framework (C43, C49-C50) of PGAM's physiological function, accepting the new metabolic regulation model.

OpenEval R7 includes mechanistic context claim C43 about serine synthesis pathway. Peer review R12 also references C43 as part of accepting the overall physiological function and conceptual framework of PGAM regulating serine synthesis.

OpenEval rates CAR-T/CAR-Treg applications (C51, C78-C80) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative without direct experimental validation. Peer review R13 accepts translational potential (C51) for autoimmune disorders and cancer without challenge, though acknowledging speculative nature.

OpenEval R17 addresses reconciliation with prior PGAM knockout studies (C52-C55), rating the explanation as SUPPORTED with logical reasoning about partial vs complete inhibition. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval R18 addresses established background knowledge claims (C56-C69, C74) as appropriately supported by literature. These contextual claims are not separately evaluated in peer review.
